A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RF-HGN research, with matching core methods and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, rendered figures and Appendices A–H support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulations, optimizer comparisons, zero-shot evaluations, molecular trajectories and appendix ablations, noise tests and batching experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds nonlinear-potential experiments and conditioning and message-passing analyses.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.1 adds a molecular-specific absolute-displacement edge encoding where v2 specified signed displacements. Appendix F introduces recursive sum/mean-pooling variants for ablation. The central random-feature construction and linear readout remain intact; regularization was already documented in v2 Appendix D.

E1.justification: New Section 4.3 adds anharmonic-oscillator and Morse-potential chain simulations, including forced, long-horizon zero-shot evaluation from five to ten nodes. These introduce distinct nonlinear interaction laws beyond the retained harmonic-chain, lattice, Lennard-Jones and closed-chain benchmark coverage.

E2.justification: The optimizer and seven architecture comparator sets are retained, alongside the existing RF-HNN, ELM and RFF comparisons. Table 3 extends Adam/ELM/SWIM comparisons to additional potentials. ELM remains evaluated in the molecular experiment despite being omitted from the selected display in Figure H.21.

E3.justification: The new potential benchmark introduces its own sample budget, 1024-wide double-precision models and 10,000-step forced rollouts at a timestep of 10^-2. Appendix F adds conditioning and one-to-six-pass evaluation protocols. Appendix C.2 also revises the reported molecular training timestep from 5^-3 to 5×10^-3; this correction alone does not establish rerunning.

E4.justification: Appendix F extends the existing width ablation with condition numbers of the least-squares matrix, testing numerical sensitivity, and recursive message-passing experiments comparing summation and averaging across one to six passes. Tables F.28–F.29 address substantial new diagnostic questions. Existing noise, batching and random-feature sensitivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain Table 1's three-run mean/minimum/maximum reporting, the disclosed exclusion of invalid SGD runs, ten-seed lattice analyses and median-model selection, and five-seed noise/batching averages with five-fold cross-validation. No changed uncertainty-estimation practice or additional significance testing is reported.

E6.justification: Table 3 adds potential-comparison results, and Tables F.28–F.29 add diagnostic outcomes. Molecular values and trajectories are revised: Table 2's final SWIM position MSE changes from 1.781e-2 to 8.301e-2, while Adam's reported model Hamiltonian changes from drifting in Table H.24 to constant at the sampled times in Table H.33. These revisions do not establish matched-setting gains. Table 1 and architecture training times remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix C.1 adds explicit anharmonic and Morse potential definitions, and Appendix F defines the conditioning diagnostic for the least-squares matrix with the bias excluded. These are limited mathematical-definition additions. Existing invariance and complexity derivations remain unchanged; the new compact Equation B.7 restates the existing forward pass.

C1.justification: The central novelty, speed/accuracy, invariance and zero-shot generalization claims are retained. The abstract's revised 150–600× wording summarizes the approximately 148–601× range already reported in v2 Section 4.1. Additional potential experiments support the existing contribution rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: v3 adds limitations concerning dynamic-edge generalization and transfer to convolution or self-attention architectures, with possible remedies involving more data or SE(3) models. Appendix F adds interpretations connecting conditioning to feature widths and summation's advantage to node-degree information. Earlier graph-type and small-system limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 documents the new benchmark's settings and molecular rollout parameters, and adds README reproduction guidance. Table D.19 separately specifies static and dynamic molecular configurations; v2 Table D.12 contained only one row despite referring to two, so an actual configuration change is unresolved. The public repository remains the same.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands random-feature history with Rosenblatt, Johnson–Lindenstrauss and Barron, and adds Bishnoi's Hamiltonian graph work. Du, Atkins and Morse are additional references supporting invariance discussion and new potentials. The principal novelty positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: v3 adds Section 4.3, renumbers the architecture benchmark, and makes localized related-work, method, limitation and reproducibility edits. Affiliations, acknowledgments and the publication header are updated. Most prose and the overall main-text and appendix organization are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds the potential-comparison table, diagnostic and settings tables, and six trajectory/snapshot figures H.10–H.15. Molecular plots are redrawn, and Figure H.21 omits ELM from that display. Numerous appendix floats move, sometimes separating them considerably from their discussion; retained figures are matched across renumbering.

improvement.justification: The additional interaction-law tests and conditioning/message-passing ablations strengthen validation, while clearer integration settings and architectural limitations improve transparency. These are bounded gains: the main comparisons and single-trajectory architecture-testing limitation remain. More fragmented appendix placement imposes a readability cost, but the added evidence and documentation support a modest net improvement.
